summary: Describes the object identifiers assigned in the arc IANA allocated to the PKIX Working Group, returns control of the arc to IANA, and sets allocation policies for future assignments.

eli5.summary: A numbered list of labels was kept by a group. This writes down what is on it and hands the list back to the official keeper.

questions: what is a pkix object identifier
what is the pkix oid arc
subtitle: A registry of object identifiers allocated to the PKIX Working Group.

tldr.problem: The PKIX Working Group needed a way to assign object identifiers (OIDs) for use in X.509 certificate extensions, algorithms, and other security mechanisms, but this required centralizing the allocation and management of an OID arc.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7299 documents all OIDs that were assigned within the PKIX arc (allocated by IANA), returns control of the arc to IANA, and establishes clear allocation policies for any future assignments within that arc.
tldr.outcome: The PKIX OID arc is now managed by IANA with defined policies, allowing the PKIX community to request new OID assignments through a standardized process and preventing conflicts or duplicate allocations.
tldr.outcomeLabel: IANA now manages the OID arc

today: RFC 7299 is Informational and current. The PKIX OID arc continues to be managed by IANA, with RFC 9158 updating some aspects of PKIX management.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Public-Key Infrastructure using X.509 (PKIX) is the framework for digital certificates and public key cryptography on the Internet. PKIX protocols and structures use object identifiers (OIDs)—sequences of numbers like 1.2.840.113549—to label different types of certificates, extensions, algorithms, and data structures.

When the PKIX Working Group was chartered, the Internet Assigned Numbers Authority (IANA) allocated a specific OID arc—a numbered namespace—for exclusive use by that group. This document describes which OIDs were assigned within that arc and establishes how future assignments will be managed. Unlike some registry documents that merely list past allocations, this RFC returns control to IANA and defines governance for the future.
sections.eli5: Security certificates use numbered labels to mark different parts. A group that works on this got their own set of numbers to use. This document says what labels they made and gives the numbering system back to IANA.

sections.title: Subordinate Object Identifier Arcs
sections.content:
The PKIX arc is defined in ASN.1 notation as: id-pkix OBJECT IDENTIFIER ::= { iso(1) identified-organization(3) dod(6) internet(1) security(5) mechanisms(5) pkix(7) }. This base arc serves as the root for dozens of subordinate arcs.

Within the PKIX arc, 25 major subordinate arcs were allocated, numbered from 0 to 23 and 48. These arcs organize different categories: module identifiers (0), certificate extensions (1), policy qualifiers (2), extended key purposes (3), CMP information types (4), CRMF registration controls (5), algorithms (6), CMC controls (7), certificate policies (14), and many others. Each subordinate arc can then have its own numbered assignments.

For example, the certificate extensions arc (id-pe, number 1) contains dozens of different extension types. The algorithms arc (id-alg, number 6) contains OIDs for cryptographic algorithms. This hierarchical structure allows the PKIX community to organize and allocate identifiers without risk of collision.
sections.eli5: The numbering system branches like a tree. The main branch is PKIX, and it splits into smaller branches like one for extensions, one for algorithms, and one for each kind of security thing.

sections.title: IANA Considerations and Registry Management
sections.content:
RFC 7299 updates the IANA SMI Security for Mechanism Codes registry to reflect the PKIX arc allocation. More importantly, it establishes 34 separate IANA registries within the PKIX namespace, each with its own allocation policies. For example, the SMI Security for PKIX Certificate Extension registry defines how new certificate extension OIDs will be assigned in the future.

The document specifies that IANA is the sole authority for future allocations within the PKIX arc. Requests for new OIDs must go through IANA using the defined processes. This prevents the working group (or any vendor) from unilaterally creating new OIDs that might conflict with allocations elsewhere. The registry structure is designed to be stable and long-lived, even if the PKIX Working Group eventually closes or shifts focus.
sections.eli5: Now that the list is written down, IANA keeps it. If someone wants a new number, they ask IANA and IANA writes it in the right place.

sections.title: Impact on PKIX Standards and Implementations
sections.content:
This registry is essential for the entire PKIX ecosystem. Whenever an RFC defines a new certificate extension, key usage, or algorithm that PKIX implementations should recognize, it must request an OID from the appropriate PKIX registry. X.509 certificate software relies on OIDs to understand what each extension means and how to process it.

By documenting all existing allocations and establishing clear policies, RFC 7299 ensures that new PKIX standards can reference stable, globally unique identifiers. Vendors implementing certificate software know they can safely use PKIX OIDs defined in this registry because IANA guarantees no conflicts. The registry also serves as historical documentation, showing which organizations and working groups have reserved numbers for which purposes.
sections.eli5: Every time someone makes a new security feature, it needs a number. This document makes sure everyone can get a unique number that nobody else is using.
